The ones that are not imputed are sex with a client, 1.8(j), and 1.7(a)(2) personal-interest conflicts. The class quiz: Amir's religious objection to suing the church is not imputed if he does no work on the matter and his beliefs create no significant risk of limiting Leona's representation, 1.10 Comment 3.

Situational rebuttal two: the mobile lawyer's actual knowledge, 1.9(b). A lawyer who changes jobs brings to, and imputes within, the new firm only confidential information the lawyer personally knew. It has no effect on concurrent conflicts. The class quiz: Lulu, whose conflict was purely imputed at her old firm and who acquired no material information about the adverse party, needs no screen, 1.9(b) Comment 5.

Situational rebuttal three: everyone who knew has left, 1.10(b). Every lawyer exposed to the client's information must have left, and no trace of it, paper or digital, may remain. It applies only to successive conflicts, never concurrent ones.

segments.ask: A lawyer at Firm A worked extensively on Client X's defense in a fraud suit. She moves to Firm B, which represents the plaintiff in that same suit. X refuses consent. Can Firm B continue?
segments.answer: Yes, if Firm B timely screens her and gives her no part of the fee, promptly gives X written notice with the required contents, and provides certifications of compliance. That is 1.10(a)(2). Otherwise her conflict is imputed to all of Firm B.

segments.ask: A partner in a firm's Chicago office represents a bank in a loan matter. A partner in the firm's Miami office, who has never heard of the bank, wants to sue it for a new client. Allowed without consent?
segments.answer: No. Imputation under 1.10(a) runs across offices and states, and a concurrent conflict cannot be screened. Both clients must consent.

segments.ask: All the lawyers who represented Client Y have left the firm, and no files remain. The firm now wants to sue Y in a substantially related matter. Allowed?
segments.answer: Yes, under 1.10(b), because no remaining lawyer has material confidential information, and Y is a former client of the firm.

segments.ask: A lawyer's spouse is the CEO of a company the firm wants to sue. The lawyer will do no work on the matter. Is his conflict imputed?
segments.answer: Probably not. It is a personal-interest conflict, and under 1.10(a)(1) it is not imputed if it presents no significant risk of materially limiting the other lawyers.

segments.say: Traps. Screens never cure concurrent conflicts. A lateral screen needs notice and certifications, not just a wall. 1.10(b) needs everyone who knew to be gone. And 1.8(k), not 1.10, imputes most 1.8 conflicts.

Recap. 1.10(a): one lawyer's 1.7 or 1.9 conflict is everyone's, except non-risky personal-interest conflicts and lateral 1.9 conflicts with a screen, no fee share, notice, and certifications. 1.10(b): departed lawyers' conflicts end when no one remaining knows. 1.10(c): waiver under 1.7.

segments.ask: What three things does the 1.10(a)(2) lateral screen require?
segments.answer: A timely screen with no part of the fee; prompt written notice to the former client; and certifications of compliance.

segments.ask: Does a screen ever cure a concurrent conflict?
segments.answer: No.

segments.ask: When does 1.10(b) let a firm take a matter against a departed lawyer's former client?
segments.answer: Unless the matter is the same or substantially related and a remaining lawyer has material confidential information.

episodes.title: Ethical screens, and prospective clients under 1.18(d)

segments.say: Roadmap. What a screen is, its six features, the only four successive-conflict situations a screen alone cures, and the prospective-client screen in 1.18(d).

What a screen is, 1.0(k): timely isolation of a lawyer from any participation in a matter, through procedures reasonably adequate to protect the information. It restricts confidential information to a lawyer or a small group and keeps it from everyone else. Most conflicts cannot be cured by a screen, and a screen never cures a concurrent conflict.

Six common features, from 1.0 Comments 8 through 10, all expected. One, the screened lawyer's written undertaking not to communicate about the matter or touch its files. Two, written notice and instructions to all other firm personnel forbidding communication with the screened lawyer about it. Three, denial of access to files and information, paper and electronic. Four, periodic reminders to everyone. Five, no share of the fee where a Rule requires it: 1.10(a)(2), 1.11, 1.12, and 1.18(d). Six, timeliness: in place as soon as practical once the firm knows or reasonably should know a screen is needed.

Only four successive-conflict situations can be cured by a screen alone. One, nonlawyer staff exposed to confidential information, 1.10 Comment 4. Two, a lawyer exposed to the information before becoming a lawyer, for example as a paralegal or law clerk, also Comment 4. Three, a lateral lawyer's actual knowledge from a prior firm, under 1.10(a)(2), with notice and certifications. Four, a prospective client's information, under 1.18(d)(2).

Now 1.18(d) in full. When a lawyer has received disqualifying information from a prospective client, representation of the adverse client is still permissible in either of two ways. One, both the affected client and the prospective client give informed consent, confirmed in writing. Or two, three conditions are met, all required. The lawyer who received the information took reasonable measures to avoid exposure to more disqualifying information than was reasonably necessary to determine whether to represent the prospective client; the disqualified lawyer is timely screened from any participation and apportioned no part of the fee; and written notice is promptly given to the prospective client.

This is why intake should be limited to what you need for a conflict check and a decision. The limit is what lets the firm screen. And government lawyers under 1.11 and former judges and neutrals under 1.12 have their own screening rules, tomorrow.

segments.ask: A paralegal worked on Client Z's case at her old firm. She joins a firm suing Z in the same matter. Is her knowledge imputed to the new firm?
segments.answer: It can be cured by screening her. Under 1.10 Comment 4, nonlawyer staff exposed to confidential information can be screened.

segments.ask: A prospective client spent two hours telling a firm partner every detail of her divorce, including hidden assets, though ten minutes would have revealed the conflict. The husband's lawyer is at the same firm. Can the firm screen the partner and keep the husband?
segments.answer: Probably not. 1.18(d)(2) requires that the lawyer took reasonable measures to avoid more disqualifying information than reasonably necessary. Two hours of detail fails that. The firm needs both clients' informed consent, confirmed in writing, or must decline.

segments.ask: A firm sets up a screen for a lateral partner two months after she arrives and after she has already discussed the matter at a team meeting. Effective?
segments.answer: No. A screen must be timely, in place as soon as practical once the need is known, and she already participated.

segments.say: Recap. A screen is timely isolation through reasonably adequate procedures: written undertaking, notice to staff, file lockout, reminders, no fee share, and timeliness. Screens alone cure only four successive-conflict situations: staff, pre-lawyer exposure, lateral lawyers, and prospective clients who were properly limited.

segments.ask: What are the two routes under 1.18(d)?
segments.answer: Informed consent confirmed in writing from both clients, or limited intake plus a timely screen with no fee share and prompt written notice to the prospective client.

segments.ask: Name four of the six features of a screen.
segments.answer: Written undertaking; notice to other personnel; denial of file access; periodic reminders; no fee share where required; and timeliness.

segments.ask: Name the four situations a screen alone can cure.
segments.answer: Nonlawyer staff, pre-lawyer exposure, a lateral lawyer's knowledge under 1.10(a)(2), and properly limited prospective-client information under 1.18(d).

episodes.title: Consent, advance waivers, Sheppard Mullin, and conflict checks

segments.say: Roadmap. Abstaining versus withdrawing, the four nonconsentable conflicts, what makes consent informed, joint-representation disclosures, advance waivers, the form of consent, Sheppard Mullin versus J-M Manufacturing, conflict-check systems, and the six-step conflicts analysis.

Abstain or withdraw. No conflict, no consequences. But you can abstain only from an engagement you never took on. Once the prospective client reasonably believes you are his lawyer, you are, and a conflicted engagement then requires withdrawal, likely from every engagement creating the conflict, unless all affected clients give informed consent, confirmed in writing.

Two ways to proceed with a conflict. One, rebut imputation and staff the matter with lawyers who are not personally disqualified. Two, if the conflict is consentable, obtain all affected clients' informed consent in the required form and substance.

The four nonconsentable conflicts, any one suffices. One, the representation is prohibited by law, 1.7(b)(2). Two, it is one of the personal-interest conflicts 1.8 forbids outright. Three, it involves a claim by one client against another client the lawyer represents in the same proceeding before a tribunal, 1.7(b)(3). Four, the lawyer does not reasonably believe the lawyer can provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client, 1.7(b)(1). That belief must be subjectively held and objectively reasonable. If no reasonable client would consent, the conflict is nonconsentable.

Class quiz applications. Co-defendants Maru and Neo blame each other and have incompatible defenses, so Oscar cannot reasonably represent both, under 1.7(b)(1) and Comment 23. A braking discrepancy and different injuries between two clients from one accident need evaluation but do not automatically bar Shiva from representing both; with informed consent, confirmed in writing, and 1.7(b) satisfied, she may.

What makes consent informed. An enforceable waiver should, and arguably must, disclose four things. One, the facts and circumstances giving rise to the situation, 1.0 Comment 6. Two, the material risks of the proposed course, 1.0(e). Three, the reasonably available alternatives, including the client's absolute right to refuse consent. Four, the client's right to seek independent advice and take the time needed. The casebook recommends always advising independent counsel.

Joint representation disclosures. Jointly represented clients have no privilege against one another and, in most states, no confidentiality against one another. Say so up front, and say what happens if interests diverge: the lawyer may have to withdraw from both. The class quiz: Amity cannot give informed consent to a joint estate plan without learning of Buzz's child. Chuck must first get Buzz's authorization to disclose, and if Buzz insists on secrecy, withdraw from both rather than finish the wills while withholding material information, Comments 18, 19, and 31.

Advance waivers, 1.7 Comment 22. The effectiveness of such waivers is generally determined by the extent to which the client reasonably understands the material risks that the waiver entails. That usually requires describing the kind of conflict that later materializes. A specific, explained waiver is more likely to work than an open-ended one, and no advance waiver can authorize a future nonconsentable conflict.

When interests later diverge, the initial consent does not cover new antagonism. Continuing for one of two doctors requires both doctors' informed consent, confirmed in writing, plus compliance with duties to the departing client, Comment 29 and 1.9. Cleo, representing her own client's litigation opponent on conflicting positions about the same trade dress, should withdraw from both. And every affected client consents: Nicole may represent Orin against current firm client Morris, even in an unrelated transaction, only if both Morris and Orin consent, confirmed in writing.

The form of consent. Most states require informed consent confirmed in writing; a few require a writing signed by the client, which is the better practice everywhere. Silence is not consent. 1.0 Comment 7: obtaining informed consent will usually require an affirmative response, and a lawyer may not assume consent from silence. And disclosure comes first. Consent given before the disclosure and explanation is no consent at all.

Sheppard Mullin versus J-M Manufacturing, California, 2018. Sheppard, Mullin, Richter and Hampton took on J-M in a qui tam suit under an engagement letter with a broad advance waiver, without telling J-M that the firm was then also representing one of the public entities suing J-M, in unrelated matters. The court held the advance waiver did not cover a known, existing conflict the firm failed to disclose, so J-M's consent was not informed and the engagement agreement was unenforceable. The firm could at most seek quantum meruit fees, depending on the seriousness of the violation. The lesson: informed consent requires disclosing conflicts you know about, and boilerplate cannot waive what was not explained. The casebook notes an amicus brief arguing that big firms demand such waivers on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.

Seeing conflicts coming. Practice organizations must maintain policies, procedures, and systems to recognize and respond to conflicts before agreeing to a new engagement. A conflicts database tracks every interaction that may have created duties to anyone: clients, prospective clients, adverse parties, co-parties, and people promised confidentiality. Run the check before receiving more than the minimum information, 1.18(d)(2), and update it when parties are added, firms merge, or lawyers join, 1.6(b)(7). 5.1(a) makes partners responsible for having such a system.

Finally, the conflicts analysis in order. Six steps. One, identify every person to whom duties are owed: current, former, and prospective clients, and non-clients promised confidentiality. Two, classify the conflict: personal interest, concurrent, or successive. Three, impute it across the firm under 1.10(a) and 1.8(k), then ask whether imputation can be rebutted by situational facts or a screen. Four, ask whether it is consentable. Five, get informed consent from every affected client in the required form, or abstain or withdraw under 1.16(a)(1). Six, name the consequences: disqualification, discipline, fee forfeiture, damages.

segments.ask: A firm's engagement letter says the client waives all future conflicts of any kind. Two years later, the firm sues the client for another client in a matter substantially related to its work for the client. Is the advance waiver effective?
segments.answer: Almost certainly not. Under Comment 22, an open-ended waiver works only to the extent the client reasonably understood the material risks, and it cannot authorize a conflict that is nonconsentable or materially limits the representation. Here the firm would be using related confidences against its own client.

segments.ask: A lawyer sends a client a conflict waiver letter and asks her to reply if she objects. She never replies. Consent?
segments.answer: No. Silence is not consent. Informed consent usually requires an affirmative response, confirmed in writing.

segments.ask: A lawyer representing two spouses in estate planning learns from the husband that he has a child from an affair, and he wants it kept from his wife. What should the lawyer do?
segments.answer: Ask the husband to authorize disclosure. If he refuses, withdraw from both rather than finish plans while withholding material information from the wife.

segments.ask: A firm knows it represents a city in unrelated matters when it takes on a company the city is suing. It relies on a boilerplate advance waiver and says nothing. Effect?
segments.answer: Sheppard Mullin: consent was not informed, the engagement agreement is unenforceable, and the firm is limited at most to quantum meruit.

segments.say: Traps. Advance waivers must be specific and understood. Known conflicts must be disclosed. Silence is not consent. Consent before disclosure is no consent. And the lawyer's reasonable belief in competent representation is objective too.

Recap. Nonconsentable: prohibited by law, outright 1.8 bans, same-proceeding claims between clients, and no reasonable belief in competent and diligent representation. Informed consent discloses facts, risks, alternatives, and the right to independent advice. Six steps: identify, classify, impute, consentable, consent or withdraw, consequences.

segments.ask: Name the four nonconsentable conflicts.
segments.answer: Prohibited by law; outright 1.8 prohibitions; claims between the lawyer's clients in the same proceeding; and no reasonable belief in competent and diligent representation of each client.

segments.ask: What did Sheppard Mullin hold?
segments.answer: A boilerplate advance waiver did not cover a known existing conflict the firm failed to disclose, so the engagement agreement was unenforceable.

segments.ask: What are the six steps of conflicts analysis?
segments.answer: Identify who is owed duties; classify the conflict; impute and test rebuttal; check consentability; get proper consent or withdraw; name the consequences.

episodes.title: Day 3 cumulative quiz

segments.say: The Day 3 cumulative quiz, mixing today with earlier days. Answer out loud.

segments.ask: May a lawyer lend a litigation client money for rent?
segments.answer: No, unless the client is indigent and pro bono, and then only as a modest gift, not a loan.

segments.ask: What three writings does 1.8(a) need?
segments.answer: Terms in writing, written advice to seek independent counsel, and the client's signed informed consent.

segments.ask: May a lawyer accept a modest, unsolicited holiday gift from a client?
segments.answer: Yes.

segments.ask: Aggregate settlement: does majority approval bind the dissenter?
segments.answer: No. Each client must give informed consent in a signed writing.

segments.ask: Is a 1.8(a) prohibition imputed to partners?
segments.answer: Yes, under 1.8(k).

segments.ask: Can a lawyer sue a current client in an unrelated matter with no confidential information at risk?
segments.answer: Not without both clients' informed consent, confirmed in writing.

segments.ask: Is a contested divorce representation of both spouses consentable?
segments.answer: No.

segments.ask: What extra element does 1.18(c) add?
segments.answer: Information that could be significantly harmful.

segments.ask: Can a screen cure a concurrent conflict?
segments.answer: No.

segments.ask: What does the lateral screen require besides the wall?
segments.answer: No fee share, written notice to the former client, and certifications.

segments.ask: What is the hot-potato rule's consequence?
segments.answer: Disqualification.

segments.ask: Which 1.6(b) exception lets firms share information to check conflicts on a lateral hire?
Does a conflict require harm before a court will disqualify?
segments.answer: No.

segments.say: That's Day 3. Tomorrow, Day 4: government lawyers, the revolving door, prosecutors, the lawyer as counselor and neutral, evidence, the limits on advocacy, and candor to the tribunal. Another heavy day. Sleep on conflicts tonight.

days.title: Government lawyers, prosecutors, and ethics in advocacy

episodes.title: Spaced review of Days 1 to 3

segments.say: Welcome to Day 4. Rapid recall first, weighted toward conflicts from yesterday.

segments.ask: What are the two kinds of concurrent conflict in 1.7(a)?
segments.answer: Direct adversity, and a significant risk of material limitation.

segments.ask: Name the four requirements of 1.7(b).
segments.answer: Reasonable belief in competent and diligent representation; not prohibited by law; no claim between clients in the same proceeding; informed consent, confirmed in writing, from each affected client.

segments.ask: What three writings does 1.8(a) require?
segments.answer: Fair terms disclosed in writing; written advice to seek independent counsel; and informed consent in a writing signed by the client, including the lawyer's role.

segments.ask: Which 1.8 rule is not imputed?
What does 1.9(b) carry with a moving lawyer?
segments.answer: Only material confidential information the lawyer personally acquired.

segments.ask: What extra element does 1.18(c) require?
segments.answer: Information that could be significantly harmful to the prospective client.

segments.ask: What three parts make up the lateral screen in 1.10(a)(2)?
segments.answer: A timely screen with no fee share, prompt written notice to the former client, and certifications of compliance.

segments.ask: What did Sheppard Mullin hold?
segments.answer: A boilerplate advance waiver did not cover a known, undisclosed existing conflict, so the engagement agreement was unenforceable.

segments.ask: May a lawyer reveal confidences to prevent a client's fraud that does not involve the lawyer's services?
segments.answer: Not under 1.6(b)(2) or (b)(3), which require the lawyer's services. Unless (b)(1) applies, no.

segments.ask: What two duties stop at scope?
segments.answer: Care and candor.

segments.ask: May a client fire a lawyer without cause?
segments.answer: Yes, anytime, though the court may need to approve substitution and fees earned are owed.

segments.ask: Who decides whether to accept a plea?
segments.answer: The client.

segments.say: Today, Part Seven, government lawyers, and Part Eight, ethics in advocacy, including the heavily tested candor to the tribunal.

episodes.title: The government lawyer's client and duties

segments.say: Roadmap. Same rules with a few twists, where government lawyers may practice, identifying the government client, conflicts within government, and duties outside the Rules.

Government lawyers follow the same Rules as everyone else, plus three things. One, obligations outside the Rules that apply because they are government employees. Two, recurring situations that make the general Rules hard to apply. Three, two Rules that apply only to them: 1.11, conflicts for current and former government lawyers, and 3.8, prosecutors.

Where they may practice. State and local government lawyers need a license where they practice, like anyone else. The federal government requires a license in at least one state or D.C., and by statute, 28 U.S.C. section 517, a federal lawyer may appear in any state or federal court nationwide. Federal lawyers still follow the conduct rules of the jurisdiction or court where they appear, under the McDade Amendment, section 530B. With no tribunal involved, the rules of the licensing jurisdiction generally govern.

Identifying the client. Often it is clear: a specific state, county, city, or agency. Sometimes the lawyer represents an interest or function of government, nominally represents the agency head while really representing the agency, or personally represents an employee, but only to protect the employer's interests too. The law that creates the entity defines it: constitutions, statutes, and regulations identify the client and the official empowered to direct counsel. The Rules will not tell you who calls the shots.

Prosecutors represent the sovereign: the State, or the People. Not the district attorney personally, not the victim, not the investigating officer; those are witnesses. The victim's own private lawyer represents the victim.

Defending government actors. Governments act only through people, so suits often name employees. In an official-capacity suit, the true client is the agency, and the named official is its procedural representative. When a government lawyer represents an employee personally, for example a Bivens damages claim against a federal officer, the employee is a full client owed every duty, yet the lawyer represents her only to serve the government's interests too. Conflicts can develop midstream, so disclose and get informed consents from everyone at the outset.

Conflicts within government. Are two agencies one client? Sometimes substantive law says whether agencies are distinct enough to be different clients, so one government law office can represent one against the other. Sometimes officials agree which lawyers handle each side, and written informed consents resolve any lingering concern. Absent agreement, infer the client from reasonable expectations, weighing three factors. One, how the government client is legally defined and funded. Two, whether it has independent legal authority over the matter. Three, the extent to which the matter has broader implications for the government. Resolve doubt in favor of detailed written disclosures and consents all around. And even when two entities are not the same client, 1.7(a)(2) still bars a significant risk of material limitation.

Duties outside the Rules. Leaders of government law offices and courts often expect a higher standard of government lawyers. Specific laws apply that do not bind private lawyers: conflict-of-interest statutes, ethics-in-government laws, codes of conduct, personnel rules, and gift rules that often bar even shared meals from people with business before the agency. The class quiz: may Patty accept Derrick's offer? Maybe: besides the Rules, she must check the gift laws and other government ethics rules.

segments.ask: A crime victim tells the assistant district attorney, you're my lawyer, so do what I say about the plea deal. Is she right?
segments.answer: No. The prosecutor represents the sovereign, the State or the People. The victim is a witness. Her own private lawyer would represent her.

segments.ask: A city attorney defends the police chief, named in his official capacity. Who is the real client?
segments.answer: The city, or the agency. The named official is its procedural representative.

segments.say: Recap. Same Rules plus government-specific law and 1.11 and 3.8. Federal lawyers can appear anywhere under section 517 but follow local conduct rules under McDade. Prosecutors represent the sovereign. Official-capacity suits: the agency is the client.

segments.ask: What statute lets federal lawyers appear in any court nationwide?
segments.answer: 28 U.S.C. section 517.

segments.ask: Name the three factors for deciding whether two agencies are one client.
segments.answer: How each is legally defined and funded, whether it has independent legal authority over the matter, and how broad the government-wide implications are.

segments.ask: Who is the client of a prosecutor?
segments.answer: The sovereign: the State or the People.

episodes.title: The revolving door: Rule 1.11(a) through (c), and the four levels

segments.say: Roadmap. 1.11 covers anyone who served as a public officer or employee. Concurrent conflicts are not imputed in government. Then the former government lawyer rules in 1.11(a), (b), (c), the definition of matter in (e), and the four levels of prior government involvement.

Two preliminaries. 1.11 covers service as any public officer or employee, not only as a practicing lawyer. And concurrent conflicts are not imputed in government. An individual government lawyer may not take part in a matter adverse to her own current client, but others in her office may. 1.10 does not apply to them, per 1.10(d). 1.11 does.

Rule 1.11(a). A lawyer who formerly served as a public officer or employee, one, is subject to 1.9(c), so she may not use or reveal the government's information. And two, shall not otherwise represent a client in connection with a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially as a public officer or employee, unless the appropriate government agency gives its informed consent, confirmed in writing.

Notice what is missing from 1.11(a). There is no requirement that the new client be adverse to the government. It bars switching sides, and more: even working on the same side, for a private client, in a matter you handled personally and substantially in government.

Rule 1.11(b). When a lawyer is disqualified under (a), no lawyer in her firm may knowingly undertake or continue the matter unless two requirements are met, both required. One, the disqualified lawyer is timely screened from any participation and apportioned no part of the fee. Two, written notice is promptly given to the appropriate government agency to enable it to ascertain compliance.

Rule 1.11(c). A lawyer having information she knows is confidential government information about a person, acquired as a public officer or employee, may not represent a private client whose interests are adverse to that person in a matter in which the information could be used to that person's material disadvantage. The firm may proceed only if the disqualified lawyer is timely screened and apportioned no part of the fee. No notice requirement.

Rule 1.11(e), matter. It includes, one, any judicial or other proceeding, application, request for a ruling or other determination, contract, claim, controversy, investigation, charge, accusation, arrest, or other particular matter involving a specific party or parties; and two, any other matter covered by the agency's conflict rules. Key point: rulemaking, which involves no specific parties, is usually not a matter.

Now the four levels of prior government involvement. Level one: she participated personally and substantially in the same matter, the narrow 1.11(e) matter involving specific parties. The bar applies even if the private client's interests are not adverse to the government. Response: she is personally out unless the agency gives informed consent, confirmed in writing. The firm may proceed with a timely screen, no fee share, and prompt written notice to the agency. More measures are probably needed to make the screen effective.

Level two: no personal and substantial participation, but she has confidential government information about a third party. That means information obtained under governmental authority that the government is prohibited by law from disclosing or has a privilege not to disclose, and that is not otherwise public, like the fact that someone was secretly investigated, or a sealed indictment. It must concern a third party adverse to the new client and be usable to that party's material disadvantage. Response: she is personally disqualified; the firm may proceed with a timely screen and no fee share, under 1.11(c). No notice requirement.

Level three: she participated only in something that is not a matter, like rulemaking, or knows ordinary confidential information that is not confidential government information. A major departure from private-sector rules: no one is disqualified and no screen is required, though some firms screen anyway. She still may not use the information to the former government client's disadvantage or disclose it, under 1.9(c), and if she cannot work on the matter without doing so, she must stay out.
Level four: no involvement and no confidential information. Same as the regular rules. No conflict; nothing required.

No cooling-off period. The Model Rules turn on personal and substantial participation, not time. The class quiz: a former prosecutor is disqualified only if she participated personally and substantially in the prosecution. Adina, personally disqualified under 1.11(a)(2), must be screened, with no fee share and written notice to the Department of Labor, before her new firm can keep the wage-and-hour case. And Praveen's nonpublic Medicare data about Dr. Hildenbrant is confidential government information under 1.11(c): he should have been disqualified and screened, and he certainly could not use or share it.

segments.ask: As an EPA lawyer, Dana personally and substantially handled an enforcement action against Acme. Now in private practice, Acme wants to hire her to defend it in the same action. Acme is the side she opposed. Can she take it?
segments.answer: Not without the EPA's informed consent, confirmed in writing, under 1.11(a)(2). Her firm may take it if she is timely screened, gets no part of the fee, and the agency gets prompt written notice.

segments.ask: As a Labor Department lawyer, Ben drafted a general regulation on overtime. Now in private practice, a client wants him to challenge that regulation's application in a lawsuit. Disqualified?
segments.answer: No. Rulemaking is not a matter under 1.11(e), because it involves no specific parties. He must not use or reveal confidential information under 1.9(c).

segments.ask: At the U.S. Attorney's office, Carla saw a sealed file revealing that a businessman was under secret investigation. She never worked on it. In private practice, a client wants to sue that businessman. What result?
segments.answer: That is confidential government information under 1.11(c). She is personally disqualified if it could be used to his material disadvantage. Her firm may proceed with a timely screen and no fee share.

segments.say: Traps. No adversity is required under 1.11(a). There is no cooling-off period. Rulemaking is not a matter. And 1.11(c) screens need no notice.

Recap. 1.11(a): former government lawyers are bound by 1.9(c), and are out of any matter they handled personally and substantially unless the agency consents in confirmed writing. 1.11(b): the firm may proceed with a screen, no fee share, and written notice to the agency. 1.11(c): confidential government information about a third party disqualifies personally; screen and no fee share.

segments.ask: What does 1.11(a)(2) require, and what does it not require?
segments.answer: Personal and substantial participation in the same matter, unless the agency consents in confirmed writing. It does not require adversity to the government.

segments.ask: Define confidential government information.
segments.answer: Information obtained under governmental authority that the government is prohibited from disclosing or has a privilege not to disclose, and that is not otherwise public.

segments.ask: Is there a cooling-off period under the Model Rules?
segments.answer: No.

episodes.title: Current government lawyers and former neutrals: 1.11(d) and 1.12

segments.say: Roadmap. 1.11(d) for lawyers now in government, then 1.12 for former judges, arbitrators, mediators, other neutrals, and law clerks.

Rule 1.11(d). A lawyer currently serving as a public officer or employee, one, is subject to 1.7 and 1.9. And two, shall not do either of two things. (i) Participate in a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially while in private practice or nongovernmental employment, unless the agency gives informed consent, confirmed in writing. (ii) Negotiate for private employment with any person who is involved as a party or as lawyer for a party in a matter in which the lawyer is participating personally and substantially. Except that a law clerk to a judge, adjudicative officer, or arbitrator may negotiate as 1.12(b) allows.

Why (d)(2)(i) bars even helping the former client. 1.9(a) bars only adversity to a former client, but 1.11(d)(2)(i) bars participation altogether, to guard against using government power for the special benefit of the former client. And why revolving door: many lawyers cycle in and out of government, some more than once.

Rule 1.12(a). Except as stated in (d), a lawyer shall not represent anyone in connection with a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially as a judge or other adjudicative officer, a law clerk to one, or an arbitrator, mediator, or other third-party neutral, unless all parties to the proceeding give informed consent, confirmed in writing. Notice: all parties consent, not just the agency.

1.12(b). A judge, adjudicative officer, arbitrator, mediator, or other neutral shall not negotiate for employment with any party or lawyer for a party in a matter in which the neutral is participating personally and substantially. A law clerk may, but only after notifying the judge or other adjudicative officer.

1.12(c). If a lawyer is disqualified by (a), the firm may proceed only if two requirements are met. One, the disqualified lawyer is timely screened and apportioned no part of the fee. Two, written notice is promptly given to the parties and any appropriate tribunal.
1.12(d). A partisan arbitrator on a multimember panel may later represent that party.
Compare the consent and notice targets. Former government lawyer: the agency consents, and the agency gets notice. Former neutral: all parties consent, and the parties and the tribunal get notice.

segments.ask: A lawyer represented a developer in a zoning dispute, then joined the city attorney's office. The dispute is still going, and she wants to help the city in it. May she?
segments.answer: Not unless the city gives informed consent, confirmed in writing. 1.11(d)(2)(i) bars participating in a matter she handled personally and substantially in private practice. And 1.9 applies too.

segments.ask: A law clerk working on a case wants to interview with a firm appearing in that case. May she?
segments.answer: Yes, under 1.12(b), but only after notifying her judge.

segments.ask: A retired judge who presided over a case joins a firm that represents one party in a later phase of that same case. Can the firm continue?
segments.answer: The judge is personally disqualified unless all parties consent in confirmed writing. The firm may continue if the judge is timely screened, gets no part of the fee, and written notice goes promptly to the parties and the tribunal.

segments.ask: A government lawyer handling an investigation of a company begins job talks with the company's outside counsel. Permitted?
segments.answer: No. 1.11(d)(2)(ii) bars negotiating for private employment with a party or a party's lawyer in a matter she is handling personally and substantially.

segments.say: Recap. 1.11(d): current government lawyers are bound by 1.7 and 1.9, may not work on matters they handled in private practice without agency consent, and may not negotiate for jobs with parties or their lawyers. 1.12: former neutrals are out unless all parties consent; firms screen with notice to parties and tribunal; clerks may job-hunt after telling the judge; partisan arbitrators may later represent their party.

segments.ask: Who must consent for a former mediator to represent a party in the same matter?
segments.answer: All parties to the proceeding, confirmed in writing.

segments.ask: What must a law clerk do before negotiating for a job with a firm in a pending case?
segments.answer: Notify the judge.

segments.ask: Why does 1.11(d)(2)(i) bar even helping a former client?
segments.answer: To prevent using government power for the special benefit of the former client.

episodes.title: Special duties of prosecutors: Rule 3.8

segments.say: Roadmap. Every paragraph of 3.8, (a) through (h), then Brady and Berger. Each paragraph marks a point in the criminal process where a prosecutor must favor justice over merely winning.
The theme, from Berger versus United States: a prosecutor may strike hard blows, but is not at liberty to strike foul ones.

The prosecutor in a criminal case shall do eight things. Paragraph (a): refrain from prosecuting a charge that the prosecutor knows is not supported by probable cause. Probable cause is a floor, not a target, and the Rule is violated only when the prosecutor knows probable cause is lacking.

Paragraph (b): make reasonable efforts to assure that the accused has been advised of the right to, and the procedure for obtaining, counsel and has been given reasonable opportunity to obtain counsel. The prosecutor cannot sit idly by if the court fails to advise the accused. The class quiz: gently remind the judge that the defendant was not advised of the right to counsel and that her finances should be assessed for appointed counsel.

Paragraph (c): not seek to obtain from an unrepresented accused a waiver of important pretrial rights, such as the right to a preliminary hearing. It does not apply to an accused appearing pro se with the tribunal's approval, and it does not forbid lawful questioning of an uncharged suspect who has knowingly waived counsel and silence, Comment 2.

Paragraph (d): make timely disclosure to the defense of all evidence or information known to the prosecutor that tends to negate the guilt of the accused or mitigates the offense, and, in connection with sentencing, disclose to the defense and to the tribunal all unprivileged mitigating information known to the prosecutor, unless relieved by a protective order. This is broader than the Constitution. Brady and Giglio require disclosing material exculpatory and impeachment evidence as due process, but the Constitution requires less for impeachment evidence before a plea, United States versus Ruiz, and limits mandated disclosure of impeachment material, Strickler versus Greene. 3.8(d) has no materiality limit. Everything that tends to negate guilt or mitigate, timely.

Paragraph (e): not subpoena a lawyer in a grand jury or other criminal proceeding to present evidence about a past or present client unless the prosecutor reasonably believes three things, all required. One, the information sought is not protected from disclosure by any applicable privilege. Two, the evidence sought is essential to the successful completion of an ongoing investigation or prosecution. Three, there is no other feasible alternative to obtain the information. Unprivileged, essential, no alternative.

Paragraph (f): except for statements necessary to inform the public of the nature and extent of the prosecutor's action that serve a legitimate law enforcement purpose, refrain from extrajudicial comments that have a substantial likelihood of heightening public condemnation of the accused, and exercise reasonable care to prevent investigators, police, and others assisting the prosecutor from making statements the prosecutor could not make under 3.6 or this Rule. No perp-walk commentary.

Paragraph (g): when the prosecutor knows of new, credible, and material evidence creating a reasonable likelihood that a convicted defendant did not commit the offense, (1) promptly disclose it to an appropriate court or authority; and (2) if the conviction was obtained in the prosecutor's jurisdiction, (i) promptly disclose it to the defendant unless a court authorizes delay, and (ii) undertake further investigation, or make reasonable efforts to cause an investigation, to determine whether the defendant was convicted of an offense he did not commit.

Paragraph (h): when the prosecutor knows of clear and convincing evidence establishing that a defendant in the prosecutor's jurisdiction was convicted of an offense the defendant did not commit, seek to remedy the conviction.

Definitions for (g). Credible means a reasonable factfinder could believe it. Material means it creates a reasonable likelihood the defendant did not commit the offense, so it must bear on guilt. Impeachment or mitigation evidence is covered by 3.8(d) instead, except impeachment so devastating that it meets the standard.

The grid, by what the prosecutor knows and where the conviction was. New, credible, material evidence, conviction in the prosecutor's own jurisdiction: disclose to a court or authority, disclose to the defendant unless a court authorizes delay, and investigate or cause an investigation. Same evidence, conviction elsewhere: only disclose to an appropriate court or authority. Clear and convincing evidence of innocence, own jurisdiction: seek to remedy the conviction, plus the (g) duties. Clear and convincing, conviction elsewhere: only (g)(1) disclosure.

The class quiz: evidence that is new, credible, and material but not clear and convincing, in his own jurisdiction, triggers (g)(2): disclose to Norman and investigate, plus (g)(1) disclosure to a court or authority. The duty to seek to remedy requires clear and convincing evidence in the prosecutor's jurisdiction.
Truthfulness binds prosecutors too. Police may use some deception in interrogation, Frazier versus Cupp, but prosecutors may not lie to a suspect about the evidence, under 4.1(a) and 8.4(c).

Brady versus Maryland, 1963. The prosecution withheld a co-defendant's statement admitting that he, not Brady, did the actual killing. The Court held that suppressing evidence favorable to an accused that is material to guilt or punishment violates due process, whatever the prosecutor's good or bad faith. It is the constitutional floor that 3.8(d) builds on. Giglio versus United States, 1972, extends it to impeachment evidence, like a promise of leniency to a key witness, and United States versus Bagley, 1985, defines materiality as a reasonable probability of a different result. 3.8(d) has no materiality limit.

Berger versus United States, 1935. A federal prosecutor misstated facts, put words in witnesses' mouths, and made improper insinuations in a counterfeiting trial. The misconduct required a new trial. The prosecutor represents a sovereign whose interest in a criminal prosecution is not that it shall win a case, but that justice shall be done. He may strike hard blows, but is not at liberty to strike foul ones. It is the source of the higher standard courts expect of government lawyers.

segments.ask: A prosecutor has a witness statement that slightly undercuts the victim's identification but would not, in her view, change the outcome. Must she disclose it?
segments.answer: Yes, under 3.8(d). The Rule has no materiality limit: anything that tends to negate guilt must be timely disclosed, even if Brady might not require it.

segments.ask: A prosecutor learns of credible new DNA evidence creating a reasonable likelihood that a man her own office convicted is innocent. It is not yet clear and convincing. What must she do?
segments.answer: Under 3.8(g), promptly disclose it to an appropriate court or authority, promptly disclose it to the defendant unless a court authorizes delay, and investigate or cause an investigation. Seeking to remedy the conviction under (h) requires clear and convincing evidence.

segments.ask: A prosecutor wants to subpoena a target's former lawyer to the grand jury about the target's payment of fees. The same records are available from the bank. Permitted?
segments.answer: No. 3.8(e) requires a reasonable belief that the information is unprivileged, essential, and has no other feasible source. The bank is a feasible alternative.

segments.ask: At arraignment, the judge forgets to advise an unrepresented defendant of her right to counsel. What should the prosecutor do?
segments.answer: Gently remind the judge, under 3.8(b): reasonable efforts to assure the accused is advised of the right to counsel.

segments.say: Traps. 3.8(a) needs knowledge that probable cause is lacking. 3.8(d) is broader than Brady. Remedying a conviction under (h) requires clear and convincing evidence and the prosecutor's own jurisdiction. Police may deceive; prosecutors may not lie.

Recap. 3.8: (a) no charges known to lack probable cause; (b) assure the right to counsel; (c) no waivers from unrepresented accused; (d) disclose all exculpatory and mitigating information; (e) subpoena lawyers only if unprivileged, essential, and no alternative; (f) no condemning publicity; (g) new, credible, material evidence of innocence: disclose, and if your jurisdiction, tell the defendant and investigate; (h) clear and convincing evidence in your jurisdiction: seek to remedy.

segments.ask: How does 3.8(d) differ from Brady?
segments.answer: 3.8(d) has no materiality limit. It covers everything that tends to negate guilt or mitigate.

segments.ask: What three beliefs must a prosecutor hold to subpoena a lawyer about a client?
segments.answer: The information is unprivileged, essential to an ongoing investigation or prosecution, and there is no other feasible way to get it.

segments.ask: What did Berger versus United States say?
segments.answer: The sovereign's interest is not that it win, but that justice be done. Hard blows, not foul ones.

episodes.title: The lawyer as counselor and neutral: 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, and 3.9

segments.say: Roadmap. The advisor rule, evaluations for third persons, the lawyer as third-party neutral, and the advocate in nonadjudicative proceedings.

Rule 2.1. In representing a client, a lawyer shall exercise independent professional judgment and render candid advice. In rendering advice, a lawyer may refer not only to law but to other considerations such as moral, economic, social, and political factors that may be relevant to the client's situation. Shall exercise independent judgment and give candid advice. May refer to non-legal factors. Comment 1: do not soften advice because the client won't like it. Comment 2: purely technical legal advice can be inadequate. When a client proposes something unlawful, 2.1 is the license for extra-legal advice about whether it is wise. The client still decides objectives.

Rule 2.3. Paragraph (a): a lawyer may evaluate a matter affecting a client for someone other than the client if the lawyer reasonably believes the evaluation is compatible with other aspects of the relationship. Paragraph (b): when the lawyer knows or reasonably should know the evaluation is likely to affect the client's interests materially and adversely, the lawyer shall not provide it unless the client gives informed consent. Paragraph (c): except as disclosure is authorized in connection with the report, information relating to the evaluation is otherwise protected by 1.6.

Examples: a title opinion for a purchaser, an opinion letter for a lender, an audit-response letter. Whether the lawyer owes the third person a legal duty is a question of other law, Comment 3, and the casebook treats such reliance as one way to assume a duty of care to a non-client. Distinguish an evaluation from investigating a non-client, for example the vendor's title for the purchaser, Comment 2.

Rule 2.4. Paragraph (a): a lawyer is a third-party neutral when helping two or more non-clients resolve a dispute or other matter, as arbitrator, mediator, or similar. Paragraph (b): the neutral shall inform unrepresented parties that the lawyer is not representing them, and when the lawyer knows or reasonably should know a party does not understand the role, shall explain the difference between a neutral and a lawyer who represents a client. Later representing a party in the same matter is governed by 1.12. And lawyers representing clients in ADR follow the Rules: candor under 3.3 in binding arbitration, which is a tribunal; otherwise 4.1, Comment 5.

Rule 3.9. A lawyer representing a client before a legislative body or administrative agency in a nonadjudicative proceeding, like lobbying, rulemaking, or hearings, shall do two things, both required. One, disclose that the appearance is in a representative capacity. Two, conform to 3.3(a) through (c), 3.4(a) through (c), and 3.5. It applies to official hearings or meetings where the lawyer presents evidence or argument, not to bilateral negotiations with the government, Comment 3.

segments.ask: A company's lawyer is asked by a bank to write an opinion letter about the company's legal standing, for the bank's loan decision. The lawyer knows the honest opinion will hurt the company's chances. May he give it?
segments.answer: Only with the company's informed consent, under 2.3(b), because he knows the evaluation is likely to affect the client's interests materially and adversely.

segments.ask: A lawyer mediating a dispute between two unrepresented neighbors notices one thinks she is his lawyer. What must he do?
segments.answer: Under 2.4(b), explain the difference between a neutral and a lawyer who represents a client, and that he is not representing her.

segments.ask: A lawyer testifies for a trade association at a legislative committee hearing on a bill. What must she do?
segments.answer: Under 3.9, disclose that she appears in a representative capacity, and comply with 3.3(a) through (c), 3.4(a) through (c), and 3.5.

segments.say: Recap. 2.1: independent judgment and candid advice, with moral and other factors allowed. 2.3: evaluations for others if compatible, with informed consent when likely to hurt the client, and 1.6 otherwise. 2.4: neutrals must tell unrepresented parties they are not their lawyer. 3.9: disclose the representative capacity and follow core candor and fairness rules.

segments.ask: What may a lawyer refer to under 2.1 besides law?
segments.answer: Moral, economic, social, and political factors.

segments.ask: Is binding arbitration a tribunal for purposes of 3.3?
segments.answer: Yes.

segments.ask: What two things does 3.9 require?
segments.answer: Disclose the representative capacity, and conform to 3.3(a) to (c), 3.4(a) to (c), and 3.5.

episodes.title: Gathering and handling evidence: 3.4 and 4.4(a)

segments.say: Roadmap. The officer of the court, investigating lawfully under 4.4(a), discovery conduct under 3.4(c) and (d), retaining and handling evidence under 3.4(a), (b), and (f), litigation holds and Zubulake, and evidence handed to you.

Being an officer of the court brings three ideas into play. One, advocacy may draw extra scrutiny. Two, courts expect behavior beyond the minimum demands of the Rules. Three, loyalty to the client is constrained by enforceable duties owed to the court and the legal system.

Investigate lawfully. 4.4(a): in representing a client, a lawyer shall not use methods of obtaining evidence that violate the legal rights of a third person, like trespass, wiretapping, or intrusion into seclusion. The class quiz: an investigator videotaping a supposedly housebound plaintiff from a public street probably does not violate 4.4(a), unless local law forbids it. The lawyer answers for an investigator's unlawful methods under 5.3 and 8.4(a). Prosecutors may not lie to a suspect about the evidence, saying the video shows you in the bank when it is impossible to tell. And a prosecutor threatening to circulate humiliating photographs of a minor to coerce cooperation uses means with no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, violating 4.4(a).

Discovery conduct, 3.4(c) and (d). A lawyer shall not, (c), knowingly disobey an obligation under the rules of a tribunal, except for an open refusal based on an assertion that no valid obligation exists. Or, (d), in pretrial procedure, make a frivolous discovery request or fail to make reasonably diligent effort to comply with a legally proper discovery request by an opposing party. Discovery misconduct is a disciplinary violation as well as sanctionable.

Class quiz applications. Openly refusing to produce the secret soda formula on the ground that no valid obligation exists is not a 3.4(c) violation, though contempt or sanctions may follow so the issue can be reviewed. But citing an unpublished opinion in violation of the court's rule violates 3.4(c), even though the brief candidly called it unpublished.

Retaining and handling evidence. A lawyer shall not, 3.4(a), unlawfully obstruct another party's access to evidence, or unlawfully alter, destroy, or conceal a document or other material having potential evidentiary value, or counsel or assist another to do so. 3.4(b): falsify evidence, counsel or assist a witness to testify falsely, or offer an inducement to a witness that is prohibited by law. 3.4(f): request a person other than a client to refrain from voluntarily giving relevant information to another party, unless two conditions are met: the person is a relative, employee, or other agent of the client, and the lawyer reasonably believes the person's interests will not be adversely affected.

Two words in 3.4(a) matter. Unlawfully: lawyers lawfully withhold all the time, through proper discovery objections, instructions not to answer privileged questions, and advising a client not to talk to police. Potential: the material need not be admissible or requested; it need only be relevant to or potentially useful in a pending or reasonably foreseeable proceeding.

Consequences for the client: monetary sanctions, then evidentiary or terminating sanctions after an order compelling discovery; and for lost material that should have been preserved, remedial measures even without bad faith, like failing to halt automatic deletion. Counsel's own duty: many courts impose personal obligations on lawyers for their clients' preservation and production. Become actively involved immediately on retention, and circulate a litigation hold to everyone who may have relevant material.

Zubulake versus UBS Warburg, Southern District of New York, 2004, Judge Scheindlin. In an employment discrimination suit, UBS employees deleted relevant emails and failed to produce others despite counsel's instructions to preserve them. The court held counsel must issue a litigation hold, communicate with key players, and monitor compliance, and it gave an adverse-inference instruction for the lost emails. Preservation is not the client's job alone.

Evidence handed to you. You may not conceal, destroy, or alter it, or counsel anyone else to. The class quiz: driving the client's bloody knife to another town and throwing it in a dumpster is unlawful concealment and destruction, a clear 3.4(a) violation and likely obstruction, and no proceeding need be pending. A note the outline marks as outside the class materials, so verify it: many courts hold a lawyer who takes possession of physical evidence of a crime may keep it a reasonable time for examination, but must then turn it over to the authorities.

segments.ask: A company's in-house lawyer, anticipating a lawsuit, tells IT to keep the automatic ninety-day email deletion running because it is standard practice. Problem?
segments.answer: Yes. Once litigation is reasonably foreseeable, material of potential evidentiary value must be preserved. Under Zubulake, counsel must issue and monitor a litigation hold. Letting deletion continue risks 3.4(a) and sanctions, even without bad faith.

segments.ask: A defense lawyer asks her client's employee, and separately a neutral eyewitness, not to talk to the plaintiff's lawyer. Permitted?
segments.answer: As to the employee, yes, if she reasonably believes his interests won't be harmed, under 3.4(f). As to the neutral eyewitness, no.

segments.ask: A lawyer believes a discovery order is invalid and openly tells the court she will not comply so she can seek review. Violation of 3.4(c)?
segments.answer: No. An open refusal based on an assertion that no valid obligation exists is excepted, though she may face contempt or sanctions.

segments.say: Recap. 4.4(a): no evidence-gathering that violates third persons' rights. 3.4(a): no unlawful obstruction, alteration, destruction, or concealment of potential evidence. 3.4(b): no falsifying or prohibited inducements. 3.4(c): obey tribunal rules except open refusal. 3.4(d): no frivolous discovery, and diligent compliance. 3.4(f): only client agents may be asked not to talk, and only if not harmed.

segments.ask: What does Zubulake require of counsel?
segments.answer: Issue a litigation hold, communicate with key players, and monitor compliance.

segments.ask: What are the two conditions in 3.4(f)?
segments.answer: The person is a relative, employee, or agent of the client, and the lawyer reasonably believes the person's interests won't be adversely affected.

segments.ask: Does 3.4(a) require that a proceeding be pending?
segments.answer: No. Potential evidence for a pending or reasonably foreseeable proceeding is covered.

episodes.title: Inadvertent documents, decorum, and criticizing judges: 4.4(b), 3.5, and 8.2

segments.say: Roadmap. What to do with an inadvertently sent document under 4.4(b) and Federal Rule 26(b)(5)(B), the four paragraphs of 3.5, and statements about judges under 8.2.

Rule 4.4(b). A lawyer who receives a document or electronically stored information relating to the representation of the lawyer's client and knows or reasonably should know that it was inadvertently sent shall promptly notify the sender. That is the whole Model Rule duty. Whether to return it, stop reading, or delete it is left to other law and professional judgment, Comments 2 and 3. Metadata is covered: track-changes comments in produced files trigger only the duty to notify.

Federal Rule 26(b)(5)(B) adds duties in federal civil cases. Once notified of a privilege claim, the receiving party must promptly return, sequester, or destroy the material, not use or disclose it until the claim is resolved, and may present it to the court under seal. Both may apply. The ABA's views have evolved from return it unread to just notify, and states vary widely; some stricter states disqualify counsel who exploit privileged material.

The class quiz: opposing counsel's email to his client, sent to you by mistake, Dear Cynthia. Promptly notify the sender, and do not contact his represented client, 4.2. And protect your own documents: know what metadata your software embeds, and scrub documents before they leave the firm.

Rule 3.5. A lawyer shall not do any of four things. (a) Seek to influence a judge, juror, prospective juror, or other official by means prohibited by law. (b) Communicate ex parte with such a person during the proceeding unless authorized by law or court order. (c) Communicate with a juror or prospective juror after discharge of the jury if any one of three is true: the communication is prohibited by law or court order; the juror has made known a desire not to communicate; or the communication involves misrepresentation, coercion, duress, or harassment. (d) Engage in conduct intended to disrupt a tribunal.

Applications. Officials include court reporters: offering a reporter a thousand dollars to fix the deposition transcript violates 3.5(a), even though she refused. Post-trial: a juror who said on the record she did not want to talk cannot be asked for feedback, even in a chance coffee-shop meeting. Disruption includes depositions, Comment 5: baseless objections to every question and improper instructions not to answer violate 3.5(d), and 3.1 and 3.4(c) and (d) too. Abusive judges, Comment 4: a lawyer may stand firm against abuse by a judge but should avoid reciprocation. Finish professionally, then report the judge under 8.3(b).

Rule 8.2(a). A lawyer shall not make a statement the lawyer knows to be false, or with reckless disregard as to its truth or falsity, concerning the qualifications or integrity of a judge, adjudicatory officer, public legal officer, or candidate for judicial or legal office. 8.2(b): a lawyer running for judicial office must follow the Code of Judicial Conduct. The standard borrows from New York Times versus Sullivan, and opinions based on disclosed facts are generally protected, Standing Committee versus Yagman, Ninth Circuit, 1995. But courts tend to read the protection narrowly.

segments.ask: A lawyer receives, by mistake, the opposing party's privileged strategy memo in a state-court case. Under the Model Rules, what must she do? Must she return it unread?
segments.answer: She must promptly notify the sender under 4.4(b). The Model Rules leave returning, reading, or deleting to other law and her judgment, though local law or a court may impose more.

segments.ask: After a verdict, a lawyer calls a juror who, at discharge, told the court she did not want to discuss the case. He is polite. Violation?
segments.answer: Yes, under 3.5(c)(2). The juror made known a desire not to communicate.

segments.ask: Before trial, a lawyer emails the judge, without copying opposing counsel, to argue a pending motion. Violation?
segments.answer: Yes, an ex parte communication under 3.5(b), unless authorized by law or court order.

segments.ask: A lawyer writes a blog post calling a judge corrupt, knowing there is no basis. Violation?
segments.answer: Yes, 8.2(a): a statement about a judge's integrity made knowing it is false, or with reckless disregard.

segments.say: Recap. 4.4(b): promptly notify the sender; anything more is other law. 3.5: no improper influence, no ex parte contact, no post-discharge juror contact that is barred, unwanted, or coercive, and no disruption. 8.2(a): no knowing or reckless false statements about judges' qualifications or integrity.

segments.ask: What is the only Model Rule duty for inadvertently sent documents?
segments.answer: Promptly notify the sender.

segments.ask: Name the three bars on post-discharge juror contact.
segments.answer: Prohibited by law or court order; the juror made known she doesn't want to talk; or misrepresentation, coercion, duress, or harassment.

segments.ask: How should a lawyer respond to an abusive judge?
segments.answer: Stand firm but avoid reciprocation, finish professionally, then report under 8.3(b).

episodes.title: Meritorious claims, adverse authority, and trial publicity: 3.1, 3.2, 3.3(a)(2), and 3.6

segments.say: Roadmap. Frivolousness under 3.1, expediting litigation under 3.2, miscitation and adverse authority under 3.3(a)(1) and (a)(2), then trial publicity under 3.6 with its seven safe harbors, the right of reply, the six presumptively prejudicial subjects, and Gentile.

Rule 3.1. A lawyer shall not bring or defend a proceeding, or assert or controvert an issue in it, unless there is a basis in law and fact for doing so that is not frivolous, which includes a good-faith argument for an extension, modification, or reversal of existing law. And the exception: a lawyer for a criminal defendant, or a respondent in a proceeding that could result in incarceration, may nevertheless defend so as to require that every element of the case be established.

Say so when you argue for a change in the law. The class quiz: with no binding authority on point, only district court and out-of-circuit decisions, Kalina is arguing an open question, not seeking a reversal, and need not disclose the non-controlling cases. And the one defense always allowed: a criminal defendant may put the state to its proof on every element, however overwhelming the evidence.

Rule 3.2: make reasonable efforts to expedite litigation consistent with the client's interests. Delay for its own sake, for financial gain, or to frustrate an opponent is not a legitimate interest, Comment 1. Compare Federal Rule 11, section 1927, and 4.4(a).

Miscitation and adverse authority. 3.3(a)(1): do not knowingly make a false statement of law to a tribunal. Discipline requires actual knowledge, not carelessness, but sloppy or misleading argument costs credibility. 3.3(a)(2): disclose legal authority in the controlling jurisdiction known to be directly adverse to the client's position and not disclosed by opposing counsel. Three elements: controlling jurisdiction, directly adverse, and not disclosed by the other side. A factually identical case from another jurisdiction need not be disclosed. Controlling adverse authority must be, even if a partner reviewed the brief. Renaldo cannot bury United States versus Smith without a parenthetical, and 5.2(b) does not help on a clear duty.

Rule 3.6(a). A lawyer who is participating or has participated in the investigation or litigation of a matter shall not make an extrajudicial statement that the lawyer knows or reasonably should know will be publicly disseminated and will have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing an adjudicative proceeding in the matter.

3.6(b), the safe harbors. A lawyer may state any of the following. One, the claim, offense, or defense involved and, except when prohibited by law, the identity of the persons involved. Two, information in a public record. Three, that an investigation is in progress. Four, the scheduling or result of any step in litigation. Five, a request for assistance in obtaining evidence. Six, a warning of danger concerning a person's behavior when there is reason to believe there is a likelihood of substantial harm. Seven, in a criminal case, also: the accused's identity, residence, occupation, and family status; information necessary to aid in apprehending an accused at large; the fact, time, and place of arrest; and the identity of the investigating and arresting officers or agencies and the length of the investigation.

3.6(c), the right of reply: a statement a reasonable lawyer would believe is required to protect a client from the substantial undue prejudicial effect of recent publicity not initiated by the lawyer or client, limited to what is necessary to mitigate it. Overcorrecting destroys the right of reply. And 3.6(d): no lawyer in the same firm or government agency may make a statement prohibited by (a).

Comment 5, six presumptively prejudicial subjects. One, the character, credibility, reputation, or criminal record of a party, suspect, or witness, or the expected testimony of a party or witness. Two, in a criminal case, the possibility of a guilty plea, or the existence or contents of a confession, admission, or statement, or a refusal to make one. Three, the performance or results of any examination or test, or a refusal to submit to one. Four, any opinion as to the guilt or innocence of a defendant or suspect. Five, information the lawyer knows or reasonably should know is likely to be inadmissible and would create a substantial risk of prejudicing an impartial trial. Six, the fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime, unless accompanied by a statement that the charge is merely an accusation.

Class quiz applications. Only lawyers participating, or who participated, in the matter and their colleagues are covered; a blogging lawyer who is not involved is not covered. Only extrajudicial statements: a closing argument in a packed courtroom is not one. Telling a reporter when you'll finish calling witnesses is a safe harbor, scheduling. An opinion on guilt is not a safe harbor. A sealed indictment is not a public record. Revealing breathalyzer results on the eve of trial is presumptively prejudicial. And prosecutors have the extra limits of 3.8(f).

Gentile versus State Bar of Nevada, 1991. Hours after his client's indictment, a defense lawyer held a press conference saying the client was a scapegoat and that a police officer was the likely thief. The client was acquitted months later, and the bar disciplined the lawyer. The Court held the substantial likelihood of material prejudice standard is constitutional for lawyers in pending cases, but Nevada's safe harbor allowing a lawyer to state the general nature of the defense was void for vagueness as applied, so the discipline was reversed. It explains 3.6's structure: a prejudice standard, specific safe harbors, and the right of reply.

segments.ask: In a brief to a state intermediate appellate court, a lawyer knows of a decision from that state's supreme court directly against her position. Opposing counsel missed it. Must she cite it?
segments.answer: Yes. 3.3(a)(2): controlling, directly adverse, and not disclosed by opposing counsel. She may argue it is distinguishable or should be overruled.

segments.ask: A defense lawyer tells reporters, my client passed a polygraph, and he is innocent. Violation?
segments.answer: Likely yes. Test results and opinions on guilt or innocence are presumptively prejudicial under Comment 5, and neither is a safe harbor. Unless it is a narrowly limited right-of-reply statement under 3.6(c).

segments.ask: A prosecutor's office announces that a suspect has been arrested, where and when, and that the police department led the investigation. Violation?
segments.answer: No. The fact, time, and place of arrest and the identity of the investigating agency are 3.6(b)(7) safe harbors.

segments.ask: Facing overwhelming evidence, a criminal defense lawyer pleads not guilty and makes the state prove each element. Frivolous?
segments.answer: No. 3.1 lets criminal defense counsel require that every element be established.

segments.say: Recap. 3.1: no frivolous claims, but good-faith arguments for change are fine, and criminal defendants may put the state to its proof. 3.2: expedite. 3.3(a)(2): disclose controlling, directly adverse authority not disclosed by the other side. 3.6: no extrajudicial statements likely to materially prejudice, with seven safe harbors, the right of reply, and colleagues bound.

segments.ask: What three elements trigger the duty to disclose adverse authority?
segments.answer: Controlling jurisdiction, directly adverse, and not disclosed by opposing counsel.

segments.ask: Name four of the 3.6(b) safe harbors.
segments.answer: The claim and persons involved; public records; an investigation in progress; scheduling or results of litigation steps; requests for help getting evidence; warnings of danger; and in criminal cases, the accused's identity, help apprehending, arrest facts, and investigating agencies.

segments.ask: What did Gentile hold?
segments.answer: The substantial-likelihood-of-material-prejudice standard is constitutional, but Nevada's general nature of the defense safe harbor was void for vagueness as applied.

episodes.title: Lawyer as witness and trial conduct: 3.7 and 3.4(e)

segments.say: Roadmap. The lawyer-witness rule in 3.7 with its three exceptions and no imputation, then 3.4(e)'s three bans at trial, and the look-alike trick.

Rule 3.7(a). A lawyer shall not act as advocate at a trial in which the lawyer is likely to be a necessary witness unless any one of three exceptions applies. One, the testimony relates to an uncontested issue. Two, the testimony relates to the nature and value of legal services rendered in the case. Three, disqualification of the lawyer would work substantial hardship on the client. And 3.7(b): a lawyer may act as advocate at a trial in which another lawyer in the firm is likely to be called as a witness, unless 1.7 or 1.9 precludes it.

Why the rule exists: the jury may confuse the roles of advocate and witness. That is also why it is not imputed: a colleague may try the case while you testify. Client consent, admissibility, or being called by the other side are not exceptions.

(a)(2) means your own fees in this case. Testifying as a damages expert on what the plaintiff-lawyer would have earned is not covered. Testifying in your own pro se fee suit is. 3.7 applies to bench trials too, though the confusion risk is lower. And note: 3.7 is about acting as advocate at trial. It does not bar pretrial work.

Rule 3.4(e). In trial, a lawyer shall not do any of three things. One, allude to any matter the lawyer does not reasonably believe is relevant or that will not be supported by admissible evidence. Two, assert personal knowledge of facts in issue except when testifying as a witness. Three, state a personal opinion as to the justness of a cause, the credibility of a witness, the culpability of a civil litigant, or the guilt or innocence of an accused.

Class quiz applications. Referring in closing to a conviction the judge excluded violates the first clause, even with a certified copy in hand. Asking, aren't you a wife-beating, pill-popping alcoholic, with no factual basis, violates the first clause; withdrawn, a curative instruction, or acquittal does not cure it. Reciting an unadmitted hearsay statement in closing violates the first clause, though it supplied a good-faith basis to ask on cross. Thank you for your honest testimony, in front of the jury, vouches for credibility, violating the third.

Trickery. Secretly seating a look-alike at counsel table to bait a misidentification misleads the tribunal, violating 3.3, 3.4, 3.5(d), and 8.4(c) and (d). That is United States versus Thoreen. Ordinary cross and argument about weak identification are fine.

segments.ask: A lawyer personally witnessed the contract signing at the center of a disputed case and is the only witness to the oral side deal. The client consents to him trying the case anyway. Permitted?
segments.answer: No. He is likely a necessary witness on a contested issue. Client consent is not an exception. A partner in his firm may try the case under 3.7(b), absent a 1.7 or 1.9 conflict.

segments.ask: In closing, a prosecutor says, I believe this defendant is guilty. Violation?
segments.answer: Yes, 3.4(e): a personal opinion on the guilt of an accused.

segments.ask: A lawyer is likely to testify only to authenticate a document both sides agree is genuine. May she try the case?
segments.answer: Yes. 3.7(a)(1): testimony on an uncontested issue.

segments.say: Recap. 3.7: no advocate who is a necessary witness, except uncontested issues, the value of legal services in the case, or substantial hardship; not imputed. 3.4(e): at trial, no alluding to irrelevant or unsupported matters, no personal knowledge, and no personal opinions on justness, credibility, culpability, or guilt.

segments.ask: Name the three 3.7(a) exceptions.
segments.answer: Uncontested issue; the nature and value of legal services in the case; substantial hardship to the client.

segments.ask: Is the 3.7 bar imputed to the firm?
segments.answer: No, unless 1.7 or 1.9 precludes it.

segments.ask: Name the three 3.4(e) bans.
segments.answer: Alluding to irrelevant or unsupported matters, asserting personal knowledge of facts in issue, and stating personal opinions on justness, credibility, culpability, or guilt.

episodes.title: Candor to the tribunal, part one: Rule 3.3 and false evidence

segments.say: Roadmap. The full text of 3.3, the ban on false statements and false evidence, the 3.4(b) versus 3.3(a)(3) contrast, witness preparation, and paying witnesses. This is one of the most tested rules in the course.

Rule 3.3(a). A lawyer shall not knowingly do three things. One, make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal, or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal by the lawyer. Two, fail to disclose legal authority in the controlling jurisdiction known to the lawyer to be directly adverse to the client's position and not disclosed by opposing counsel. Three, offer evidence that the lawyer knows to be false.

Then, still in (a)(3): if a lawyer, the lawyer's client, or a witness called by the lawyer has offered material evidence and the lawyer comes to know of its falsity, the lawyer shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal. And: a lawyer may refuse to offer evidence, other than the testimony of a defendant in a criminal matter, that the lawyer reasonably believes is false.

Rule 3.3(b). A lawyer representing a client in an adjudicative proceeding who knows that a person intends to engage, is engaging, or has engaged in criminal or fraudulent conduct related to the proceeding shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the tribunal. Note: any person, not only the client. Bribing a juror, for example.
Rule 3.3(c). The duties in (a) and (b) continue to the conclusion of the proceeding, and apply even if compliance requires disclosure of information otherwise protected by 1.6.

Rule 3.3(d). In an ex parte proceeding, a lawyer shall inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the lawyer that will enable the tribunal to make an informed decision, whether or not the facts are adverse.
Why 3.3 exists: the tribunal depends on the advocates. When the system's integrity and the client's confidence collide, 3.3 picks the system. That is the one place confidentiality loses outright.

Don't lie, and don't present false evidence.
